title: Mammalian Cell Cryopreservation

references.label: General microbiology/molecular biology laboratory manuals (ASM curriculum resources)

purpose: To freeze and store viable cells long-term in liquid nitrogen (or equivalent ultra-low temperature storage), preserving a stock that can later be thawed and recovered for continued culture.
principle: Water forming sharp ice crystals during freezing can physically rupture cell membranes and organelles; a cryoprotectant (commonly DMSO or glycerol) lowers the freezing point and promotes the formation of smaller, less damaging ice crystals, while a controlled, gradual cooling rate (commonly around -1°C per minute down to a low intermediate temperature) allows cells time to lose intracellular water osmotically before it can freeze internally, both of which substantially improve post-thaw viability compared to uncontrolled freezing.
requiredMaterials: Controlled-rate freezing container or device (e.g. an isopropanol-based freezing container achieving an approximately -1°C/minute cooling rate)
Liquid nitrogen or ultra-low-temperature freezer for long-term storage
requiredReagents: Freezing medium containing an appropriate cryoprotectant (e.g. DMSO) in complete growth medium or serum

procedure.instruction: Harvest a healthy, actively growing culture and determine cell concentration and viability.
Centrifuge to pellet cells and resuspend in cold freezing medium at the target cell concentration per cryovial.

Aliquot the cell suspension into labeled cryovials promptly, minimizing the time cells spend in cryoprotectant-containing medium at room/ambient temperature before freezing begins, since many cryoprotectants are toxic to cells with prolonged exposure at warmer temperatures.
Place vials into a controlled-rate freezing container or device and transfer to a -80°C freezer (or the device's specified process) to achieve a gradual, controlled cooling rate.
After the recommended time at -80°C, transfer vials to long-term liquid nitrogen (vapor or liquid phase) storage for extended preservation.
Record vial identity, passage number, cell count, and storage location in the lab's inventory documentation.

observations: Vials reach the target intermediate temperature at the intended controlled cooling rate before long-term storage.
interpretation: Successful cryopreservation is ultimately confirmed by post-thaw viability and normal recovery when a vial is later thawed and cultured; poor post-thaw recovery can result from too slow or too fast a cooling rate, excessive cryoprotectant exposure time before freezing, or poor starting culture health.
criticalNotes: Minimize the time cells spend in cryoprotectant-containing medium before the freezing process actually begins.
Use a controlled cooling rate rather than placing vials directly into liquid nitrogen or a -80°C freezer without a controlled-rate device, which typically freezes too quickly for good viability.
precautions: Handle DMSO and other cryoprotectants per their safety data sheets, including skin contact precautions.
Use appropriate cryogenic personal protective equipment (insulated gloves, face/eye protection) when handling liquid nitrogen storage.
biosafetyNotes: Follow institutional biosafety guidance for the specific cell line during freezing, labeling, and storage.
limitations: Post-thaw recovery varies by cell type, and some cell types tolerate cryopreservation considerably better than others even with an identical protocol.
Cryoprotectant choice and concentration may need to be optimized per cell type rather than assumed universal.
